summary: Democrats were projected to win the House and Senate in the US midterms, and the Supreme Court heard a dispute over Catholic preschools and a Colorado state-funded program.

news.title: Democrats projected to win the House and Senate in the US midterms
news.tldr: The BBC and NPR report that Democrats won both chambers of Congress on November 3; President Trump said he would respect the outcome.
news.why_selected: An election result with a direct effect on how the federal government works for the final two years of a presidential term.

sections.heading: Context
sections.body: The United States held midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, halfway through President Donald Trump's second term. The BBC reported that Republicans had held unified control of Congress since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025. This summary relies on reports published early on November 4, and counts may change.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.body:
NPR reported that Democrats gained full control of Congress for the first time since 2023, winning both the House of Representatives and the Senate. The BBC said Democrats were projected to win 245 House seats to the Republicans' 166, and that Democrats flipped at least six Senate seats.

According to the BBC, Democratic Senate winners included James Talarico over Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, Adam Hamilton in Kansas, Annie Andrews in South Carolina, Josh Turek in Iowa and Sherrod Brown in Ohio. Both outlets reported that Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan, and that Troy Jackson won in Maine. In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott, both outlets said.

Trump told CBS, the BBC's US partner, that he wanted to make deals with congressional Democrats, and NPR said he later congratulated them and said more than once that he would respect the outcome. The BBC added that he also posted an image of a cap with the word "veto."

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body:
NPR's reporters said a Democratic Senate majority could slow the president's cabinet and judicial nominees, and that a Democratic House would gain subpoena power to compel witnesses to testify and could open investigations. The BBC said Democrats could frustrate Trump's agenda and that a third impeachment attempt could be possible; NPR said Democrats were cautious about pursuing one.

Explanations differed. NPR's Domenico Montanaro attributed the result to Trump's unpopularity, economic frustration and the Iran war, and noted that the Democratic Party itself remains unpopular. The BBC reported that Trump said his name was not on the ballot and that Republicans would have won decisively if it had been.

sections.heading: What to watch
sections.body: Watch whether final tallies match the projections, how Jeffries and congressional leaders organize committees and investigations, and whether Trump and Democrats reach agreement on any legislation.

news.title: Supreme Court hears Catholic preschools' challenge to Colorado's nondiscrimination rule
news.tldr: At oral argument, SCOTUSblog and NPR said a majority of justices seemed inclined to back Catholic preschools seeking an exemption from Colorado's nondiscrimination rule; no ruling yet.
news.why_selected: A major pending Supreme Court case on religious exercise, public funding and anti-discrimination law, argued within the news window.

sections.heading: Context
sections.body: In 2023, Colorado launched a universal preschool program that, SCOTUSblog reported, offers families up to 15 free hours of preschool per week at participating schools. NPR said the program was open to religious groups. To take part, schools must sign a nondiscrimination agreement covering categories including religious affiliation, sexual orientation and gender identity. Colorado reads the agreement as barring schools from declining LGBTQ families.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.body:
On Tuesday the Supreme Court heard just over two hours of argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy. The challengers are the Archdiocese of Denver, two Catholic parishes with preschools and two parents. SCOTUSblog reported that they argue the First Amendment requires an exemption from the agreement, and that the district court and the 10th Circuit rejected that claim. The Trump administration argued in support of the challengers.

SCOTUSblog said a majority seemed to agree that Colorado's refusal should face a stricter constitutional test than the lower court applied. Justice Neil Gorsuch asked whether earlier cases had been a waste of time, and Justice Brett Kavanaugh asked why the state had not sought a "win-win," noting about 2,000 participating schools and 34 Catholic ones, according to NPR.

Colorado Deputy Solicitor General Helen Norton said the state welcomes religious preschools and asks only that they follow the same rules as everyone else. Justices Elena Kagan, Ketanji Brown Jackson and Sonia Sotomayor questioned the challengers' position. Chief Justice John Roberts pressed both lawyers on how the 2022 decision in Carson v. Makin applies.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: The case tests how far earlier rulings against excluding religious schools from public funding reach when a law applies equally to every provider. Supporters of the archdiocese say the state is excluding Catholic schools for their religious exercise. The state and the three liberal justices emphasized that the rule applies equally to all participants. NPR said a decision is expected by summer 2027.

sections.heading: What to watch
sections.body: Watch for the written decision, which NPR said is expected by summer 2027, and whether the court applies the stricter test itself or sends the case back to lower courts, as SCOTUSblog said it could.
